title: Daylighting Impacts on Human Performance in School
authors: Lisa Heschong, Roger L. Wright & Stacia Okura, 2002
research_question: To demonstrate a clear relationship between the presence of daylight and human performance in buildings.

participants.description: Approximately 6,000 to 8,000 second through fifth grade students from three school districts in Orange County, CA (Capistrano), Seattle, WA, and Fort Collins, CO. Capistrano: 75% white, 17% Hispanic, 8% other ethnic groups; 15% qualify for free/reduced lunches. Seattle: 53% minority, 40% eligible for free/reduced lunch. Fort Collins: 14% minority, 21% eligible for free/reduced lunch.
participants.recruitment: Data gathered from three participating school districts.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Classroom daylighting conditions, categorized by: Window Code (0-5, based on size, tint, obstructions), Skylight Code (types A, B, based on presence, type, diffusion, control), and a combined Daylight Code (0-5, expert assessment of expected illumination levels and uniformity). Also, presence of operable windows and air conditioning type.

measures.instrument: Core Level Tests (RIT scale, fall to spring change)
Iowa Test of Basic Skills (ITBS, NCE scale, end-of-year scores)
Core Level Tests (RIT scale, end-of-year scores)
School district records (gender, ethnic background, socio-economic status, participation in special programs)
Architectural plans, aerial photographs, maintenance records, site visits (age of school, classroom size, type, population, window/skylight presence/size, operable windows, AC type)

implementation_implications: Daylighting has a statistically significant positive impact on student performance in schools.
The findings may be transferable to other building types like offices and factories.
Further controlled experiments are essential before widespread design/retrofit to increase daylighting.

limitations: The statistical analysis cannot prove causal relationships, only correlations.
The study did not include analysis of the electric lighting system due to lack of data and alterations since original construction.
Information on operable windows was not collected for Seattle and Fort Collins districts.
Insufficient daylight variation within Seattle and Fort Collins schools prevented adding a school-site variable to models for these districts.
Least amount of information about student and school characteristics was available for Fort Collins.
The weak positive effect of skylights in Fort Collins may be due to poor lighting quality from south-facing monitors and teachers keeping shades closed.
Daylight variables were based on expert evaluation of potential daylight, not actual illumination measurements over time.
Limited funds prevented sampling enough classrooms for illumination measurements.
No information on how teachers actually operated classroom lighting (on/off, blinds).
Curriculum differences between teachers were not explicitly controlled for in Seattle and Fort Collins.
Other variables associated with test performance (e.g., high expectations, principal leadership, school climate) were not explicitly controlled for.
The R² for the daylight variable was small (e.g., 0.003 for Capistrano math), suggesting a small effect size.
The analysis was presented in a way that some readers found obscure, making it difficult to accept conclusions with confidence.
